articles.title: Cabinet Approves Upgrade of NH-22 Section in Bihar - GKToday
articles.content: Home Cabinet Approves Upgrade of NH-22 Section in Bihar Cabinet Approves Upgrade of NH-22 Section in Bihar August 20, 2026 Current Affairs Today - Latest Current Affairs - 2026-2027 The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs approved the four-laning and upgradation of the 82.578 km Muzaffarpur-Sitamarhi-Sonbarsa section of National Highway-22 in Bihar on 19 August 2026. The project will be executed under the Hybrid Annuity Mode at a total capital cost of ₹3,590.73 crore. The corridor connects Muzaffarpur with the India-Nepal border at Sonbarsa through Sitamarhi. Project Alignment and Route Features The upgraded highway serves as a feeder route to NH-27 and links Sonbarsa with major commercial centres in Muzaffarpur. The corridor has been designed for a maximum speed of 100 kmph and an average operating speed of 80 kmph. The project design includes no at-grade median openings for uninterrupted traffic movement. Engineering Components and Structures The project includes seven major bridges, three railway overbridges, and two flyovers. One bridge will span 340 metres over the Bagmati River, which is a perennial river in Bihar. The two flyovers will measure 1,170 metres and 270 metres. Important Facts for Exams Hybrid Annuity Mode is a public-private partnership model used in highway development in India. National Highway-22 is a numbered national highway in India and forms part of the national road network. PM GatiShakti National Master Plan is a multi-modal infrastructure planning framework of the Government of India. The Bagmati River flows through Bihar and is associated with flood-prone plains in north Bihar. Economic and Connectivity Context The corridor covers five economic nodes, including four industrial estates and one mega food park. The project is linked with multimodal connectivity under the PM GatiShakti National Master Plan. The route also provides access to Baba Garibnath Temple, Mata Janki Temple, Janaki Punaura Dham Temple, and the Buddhist Circuit. articles.title: Shabdalok Kolkata: Inside India's First Museum Of Word - Outlook Traveller
articles.content: Shabdalok Kolkata: Inside India’s First Museum Of Word At Belvedere House, the National Library has opened India's first immersive language museum—nine galleries where visitors smell, touch and listen their way through how words shaped a civilisation By Anwesha Santra Updated on: 20 Aug 2026, 11:15 am Inside Shabdalok (Museum of Word), Kolkata : Official Website/ Museum of Word Roughly 5,400 years ago, in the marshy floodplains of southern Mesopotamia, Sumerian scribes began pressing wedge-shaped marks into wet clay to track grain and livestock. Cuneiform is widely regarded as the world's earliest known writing system, and within a few centuries Egypt had hieroglyphs, the Indus Valley had its own still-undeciphered script, and China had oracle-bone inscriptions. Writing did not invent language—speech is far older—but it did something language alone could not: it let a thought outlive the person who had it. A law, a prayer, a debt, a poem could now travel across distance and generations. Every empire, religion, and legal system that followed leaned on this trick. The Phoenician alphabet, born around the 11th century BCE, went on to seed Greek, Latin, and eventually most European scripts, while in India, Brahmi—visible today on Ashoka's 3rd-century-BCE edict pillars—became the ancestor of nearly every script the subcontinent now writes in, from Devanagari and Bengali to Tamil and Odia. Civilisation, in a very literal sense, is what got written down. India inherited an unusually large share of that story. The 2011 Census recorded 121 languages and more than 19,500 raw mother-tongue responses across the country, a diversity the Constitution tries to formally hold together through its Eighth Schedule. Framed under Articles 344 and 351, the Schedule started in 1950 with 14 languages and has grown through amendments in 1967, 1992 and 2003 to its present count of 22—Assamese, Bengali, Bodo, Dogri, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Kashmiri, Konkani, Maithili, Malayalam, Manipuri, Marathi, Nepali, Odia, Punjabi, Sanskrit, Santali, Sindhi , Tamil, Telugu, and Urdu—with three dozen more languages, including Bhojpuri and Rajasthani, still lobbying for a place on the list. It is this constitutional patchwork of tongues and scripts that Kolkata's newest cultural institution has chosen to put on public display, not as a list to memorise but as something to walk through. My Mother Tongue Gallery Photo: Official Website/ Museum of Word My Mother Tongue Gallery Photo: Official Website/ Museum of Word A Museum Built To Be Felt, Not Just Read Called Shabdalok, or the Museum of Word, it opened on July 19, 2026, inside Belvedere House on the National Library campus in Alipore, and is India's first museum devoted entirely to language. Developed by the National Library under the Union Culture Ministry, it was inaugurated by Union Home Minister Amit Shah, who called it a major step towards reviving the country's cultural heritage, and argued that language cannot exist without words born of human emotion, nor culture without language to carry it. The inaugural phase spans 12 rooms and nine galleries covering the origin of words, mother tongues, the evolution of language, oral traditions,...
